preamble: Underlining looks like a one-button job, and there is a button for it. But a button hides where the thing lives and what it belongs to. The menus show you the shape of the program: underline isn't its own feature, it's one of a small family of changes you can make to a run of text — bold, italic, strikethrough, superscript. Walk the menu once and you'll know where all its siblings live too.
generalization: Toolbar buttons are shortcuts to menu items, never the other way round. When you can't find something, or you want to know what else is near it, walk the menu — the grouping tells you how the program thinks. Everything that changes the characters themselves sits under Format > Text; everything that changes the shape of the paragraph sits a little further down the same menu.

steps.intent: You're not adding anything to the document and you're not changing the document itself — you're changing how existing characters appear. That's what Format is for: it acts on what's already selected.
hints: The text is already there. You're altering its appearance, not creating or inserting anything.
In the menu bar along the top, between Insert and Tools.

wrongHints.Insert: Insert is for putting something new into the document — an image, a link, a page break. Your text already exists; you're only changing how it's drawn.
wrongHints.Edit: Edit handles moving text around — cut, copy, paste, undo. It doesn't touch appearance.
wrongHints.View: View changes how you see the whole document on screen, not how the document itself is stored. An underline is part of the document, not part of your window.

steps.intent: Format covers a lot: paragraphs, images, tables, columns. The Text submenu narrows it to changes that apply to the characters themselves — the ones that travel with the letters wherever you move them.
hints: Format is split by what you're acting on. You're acting on letters, not on paragraphs or images.
Near the top of the Format menu, the first entry with an arrow beside it.

wrongHints.Paragraph styles: Styles set what a line *is* — a heading, body text. Underlining a few words isn't a change of meaning, it's a change to the characters.
wrongHints.Align & indent: That moves the whole paragraph around on the page. Underline stays with the letters, so it belongs with the text options.
wrongHints.Bullets & numbering: That's list structure, applied to whole lines. You want the group that acts on the characters inside a line.

steps.intent: Now you can see the family: bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, superscript. They all do the same kind of thing — mark a run of characters — which is why Docs keeps them together. Pick the one you came for, and note the keyboard shortcut listed beside it, since that's the fast route next time.
hints: One of these marks text with a line beneath it rather than through it.
Third in the list, below Bold and Italic.

wrongHints.Strikethrough: Also a line, but drawn through the middle — it conventionally means deleted or no longer true. Underline sits just above it.
wrongHints.Bold: Bold is the neighbour, and a reasonable place to land if you're scanning fast. Underline is two below it.
